newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Russian economic woes endanger rare Siberian tiger.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russian economic woes endanger rare Siberian tiger.

text.p: The world's biggest cat proudly embellishes the coat of arms of the Primorsky Krai region in Russia's Far East and of Vladivostok, its capital.

But conservationists fear that if more is not done the Siberian tiger, already listed in the United Nations' Red Book of endangered species, may go the way of the dodo in a few years and survive only as a symbol in such local insignia.

"The tiger is in a very dangerous situation today. There are only about 400 left and the numbers are declining," said Dmitry Pikunin, a veteran tiger specialist at Vladivostok's Pacific Institute of Geography.
"This past winter I had to look long and hard to find tiger tracks in places where we normally expect to see them," he said.
Pikunin fears that the tiger is fated to share the fate of another local endangered cat, the Amur leopard, whose population is put at less than 25.
TIGER THREATENED BY DEVELOPMENT, RUSSIANS' POVERTY
In a recent report the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) said the tiger's future was closely linked to the broader economic and ecological situation in Russia's Far East.

This remote region of forests, fast-flowing rivers and hot springs was largely shielded from development in Soviet times when Vladivostok, home of the Pacific Fleet, was closed to outsiders and international borders were sealed.
But the opening up of the region and keen interest in its rich resources of timber and minerals pose a powerful threat to both tiger and leopard.
"People here live very badly, there is terrible poverty, and a tiger's skin and bones can fetch high prices," said Pikunin.

He declined to specify a price but local sources say a tiger skin is worth many thousands of dollars -- a huge sum for Russians struggling to make ends meet during the country's tortuous shift from communism to a market economy.
"Poachers are by far the most serious threat to the tiger," said Pikunin, who has spent most of his career studying the cat.

Demand for the tiger's bones and organs remains strong in nearby China where they are a prized ingredient in traditional medicine. The tiger is a protected species in China as in Russia but tough penalties rarely deter the poachers.
TIGER BEING IDOLISED BY ECOLOGISTS, SOME EXPERTS SAY
But not all experts share Pikunin's pessimism about the tiger's prospects.
Viktor Gapunov of the Primorsky Krai regional government's Committee of Natural Resources said he believed the tiger population was stable and sustainable at current levels.

He even questioned the need to keep the Siberian tiger in the Red Book's first category, comprising the world's most endangered species, saying its status was secure enough to demote it to third. There are five categories in all.
"The Siberian tiger was put into the first category in 1987 when its numbers were already beginning to recover," he said.
"The tiger is a normal animal but it has been turned into an idol. Idealists with no knowledge of biology rally against any attempt to control the population," said Gapunov.
TIGER TRIGGERS POLITICAL CONTROVERSY

In a sign of how politically sensitive tiger conservation has become, the Primorsky Krai government recently threatened to sue the Fund over accusations that it had planned to allow some limited culling of the local tiger population.

Valery Shafronovsky, who is vice-president of the regional government's Committee of Natural Resources, told Reuters the accusations were completely unfounded and added that in any case only Russia's federal authorities could authorise such a cull.

The local "Vladivostok" newspaper reported that Britain's Prince Philip, husband of Queen Elizabeth and honorary president of the World Wide Fund for Nature, had kept the city off his itinerary during a recent trip to the Russian Far East due to a suspicion that Primorsky Krai was less committed to tiger conservation.
Primorsky Krai officials were angry that their efforts to protect the tiger in the face of adverse economic circumstances were being ignored or played down.
"The regional government has an annual budget deficit of 60 percent but it still finds the money to support our six nature reserves," said Shafronovsky.
He said some environmental activists wanted effectively to turn the entire Krai into a nature reserve but said such a move would do nothing to secure the tiger's future.
TIGER'S SURVIVAL HINGES ON HUNTERS AND THEIR WELL-BEING
"We have to create a compensation mechanism, a fund to help hunters and farmers who suffer directly from the tiger's predations," Shafronovsky said.
"The more secure and properous our hunters are, the more secure will be the tiger's future," he added. "Tigers and hunters are mutually dependent, their fortunes are linked."
The tiger's prey consists mainly of deer and boar but they sometimes kill cattle and goats and are especially fond of dogs. "Rural dwellers cannot get by without a dog," said Shafonovsky.
Experts say the tiger generally only attacks humans if attacked or threatened but Gapunov mentioned two incidents in the past year in which a tiger had killed people who were not trying to shoot it.
Pikunin defended the tiger against such charges.
"The tiger is a very careful, discreet animal. I have lost dogs to the tiger but I have never felt its aggression directed at me during my encounters with the animal," he said.
"I am 100 percent sure that every attack on a human being happens when somebody did something to frighten the beast."

Asked why he had devoted so much of his life to studying and observing this fearsome cat that many see doomed to eventual extinction, Pikunin smiled. "I suppose you have to have a bit of the fanatic in you."
